Introduction & Executive Summary** ##### **1.1 Introduction** With gold having posted a new record nominal high of $1,679.50 at the time of writing, the yellow metal has reported a notable gain of almost $150 since the release of our last _3-Year Gold Forecast_ (on 27th May 2011). This impressive rally has largely reflected increasing concerns over sovereign debt problems in both Europe and the United States and the consequent damage to confidence in most major currencies. The rally in the price from early July is all the more dramatic as it followed a relatively lacklustre few months for investment, as evidenced by the small growth in gold ETF holdings, limited interest in physical gold in Europe and some heavy liquidations of long positions on Comex. Nonetheless, overall investment remained firmly in positive territory (World Investment showed a net inflow of $33 billion in the first half of this year in total), thanks in part to good OTC buying and strong bar investment across Asia. This reflects the ongoing importance of other factors such as heightened inflation concerns and low interest rates. Gold prices this year have also been supported by some favourable fundamental developments. First and foremost, central banks have continued to add to their gold holdings in order to diversify official reserves away from the US dollar. After an unexpected purchase of some 100 tonnes by Mexico early this year, Korea recently confirmed that it bought 25 tonnes in June and July (its first purchase in 13 years). Basis GFMS statistics, net official sector purchases in the first half of 2011 have already totalled more than 190 tonnes, against 73 tonnes over the same period last year. In addition, scrap supply has remained moderate, with a limited response when the gold price breached $1,600 due to such factors as price accustomisation, stock depletion and bullish price expectations. Lastly, jewellery fabrication has proved surprisingly robust (chiefly in India and China), with buying linked to this area particularly strong on any dip in the gold price. Looking ahead, the fact that the gap between gold’s low and high so far this year stands at over $360 and the sudden scale of recent gains have all made for a challenging environment in which to forecast prices for the 2011-2013 period. A key reason for this is the intrusion into the economic realm of politics (arguably a far trickier area to predict) by means of the worsening sovereign debt crisis in both Europe and the United States and it seems far from likely that political overspill has run its course.  Indeed, although US leaders have already given final approval to legislation raising the country’s debt limit, the deal seems to be insufficient to quell longer term disquiet; financial markets now seem to be focusing on the growing prospect of a downgrade to the United States’ AAA credit rating as a credible policy to reduce the deficit seems distant, particularly with a background of recent poor economic news. To an extent, the eruption of this crisis has raised the prices in our **Base Case** towards levels once reserved for our most bullish variant, Scenario B. In addition to the Base Case, we also offer two alternative scenarios for the global economy that are very different to our central forecast. In each instance, these have distinct implications for the level and trajectory of gold prices over the next three years. **Scenario B** presents the most positive outlook for gold prices, with an investor led bull market continuing throughout the forecast period. It is important to stress that we have raised the probability of this scenario from 30% to 40% since the previous report, reflecting the rapid deteriorating sovereign debt situation on both sides of the Atlantic. A key difference between Scenario B and the Base Case is that the fo

rmer assumes the persistence of sovereign debt problems for the next couple of years, rather than seeing the start of resolution next year.  As a consequence of this for example, we would be highly likely to see the United States’ credit rating downgraded in the short to medium term.  In addition, with weakness persisting in the US economy, we would expect the Fed to start a further round of monetary easing and maintain interest rates at ultra-low levels over almost the entire forecast period. 

Under such circumstances, a more rapid increase in inflation rates seems to be inevitable, particularly in the United States where the CPI is forecast to rise to

5.5% by 2013.  Furthermore, it is very likely that the authorities will be tempted to tolerate a rise in inflation if this boosts GDP growth and reduces the real level of public debt.  In line with this, Scenario B also envisages a sharp drop in the value of the US dollar.  These factors should prompt a far broader move into gold among institutional investors, which in turn will result in gold prices advancing in each year of the forecast to an average of $2,090 in 2013.  That outcome is substantially higher than forecast in May, when the rally was expected to take us to $1,940 in that year. 

A complete contrast is **Scenario C** , where investment will start to slip this year.  Given the greater likelihood of a continuation of loose fiscal and monetary policies in the United States, we assign this scenario a 15% probability, 5% lower than in May.  Under this scenario, the weakness in the gold price is basis a secular recovery in the dollar and a low level of inflation, reflecting governments’ failure to boost private demand and consumer spending in advanced economies.  The prolonged period of low inflation in western countries will also be compounded by further austerity measures and tighter monetary policy at a time when economic growth is still sluggish and unemployment rates remain high.  These factors should reduce gold’s appeal to investors, most notably from 2012 onwards, when a marked reduction in investment results in prices slipping to levels that are more in line with gold’s underlying supply/demand fundamentals. 

It is of note that the gold price under this scenario has been revised upward noticeably compared with our previous forecast.  This reflects the recent pick up in investor interest and a higher likely starting point for the gold price in forthcoming years. 

Much of the above has focused on the principal economic variables and investment.  As mentioned previously, however, we do not subscribe to the view that price direction and level are determined by investment alone.  The following analysis of expected trends in the underlying supply/demand variables shows that these will also play an important, if subsidiary, role in gold price determination in 2011-13. 

###### **

1.2 The Base Case Scenario** 

Under the Base Case, **mine production** is forecast to continue rising throughout the forecast period as it posts successive records and reaches a peak of 2,957 tonnes in 2013.  This forecast is premised on an increasing number of mining companies implementing 









expansions at a number of operations.  It also reflects our growing confidence in producers’ ability to bring projects into production in a timely manner.  Despite a falling price in 2013, we still expect there to be enough momentum behind mine supply to push growth at that time, albeit at a much slower pace.  It is of note that our forecast has been revised upward modestly, mainly due the upward revision in our price forecast. 

In spite of a major increase in gold prices this year, **scrap supply** is forecast to rise by only a modest 7%.  In part, this is because expectations of further price gains have seen many consumers hold back from selling.  Furthermore, there was a degree of depletion in near market stocks in some markets, with jewellery holdings already having been liquidated, typically during previous periods of high prices.  With gold entering a declining trend at some point during 2012, scrap supply will also start to retreat, although volumes still remain very high in 2013 by historical standards. 

Turning to demand, our forecast for **jewellery** is little changed since the previous forecast.  Specifically, demand is expected to increase by a small 2% in 2011, despite rising prices.  Nevertheless, it is important to note that almost all of this growth will come from India and China, as bullish price expectations, stable growth in incomes and rising inflation have generated very healthy demand in both countries so far this year.  Excluding the two, jewellery offtake is forecast to remain generally weak, a result of elevated prices plus sluggish economic growth in western countries.  While prices will drop considerably in the latter part of the forecast, demand will rise only modestly, with its total in 2013 still well below its pre-crisis level. 

**Other fabrication** is set to increase by 7% to 807 tonnes in 2011, on the back of higher electronics and coin offtake.  Thereafter, while the former will continue to grow, the latter is forecast to decline, leaving the overall figure broadly flat in both 2012 and 2013. 

**Net official sector purchases** are forecast to rise by more than 230 tonnes to 305 tonnes this year and then average 225 tonnes in 2012-2013.  Our forecast has been revised upward since the previous report, basis the latest announcement from Korea who bought 25 tonnes in June and July coupled with ongoing robust purchases from a number of emerging market countries, including Thailand, Russia and Mexico, all of which have reported further increases in gold holdings in the second quarter of this year.

###### **1.4 Scenario C** In sharp contrast to the inflationary forecast discussed above, **Scenario C** features a notably weaker gold price trend, although prices are still expected to stay comforta bly above $1,000 by 201 3 ( basis the annual average). Nevertheless, World Investment is slated to fall back, with the rate of decline accelerating by the end of the forecast. The more subdued investment trend is clearly highlighted by its performance in value terms, which halves between 2011 and 2013. Investment under Scenario C also compares less favourably with the Base Case, as World Investment drops below 1,120 tonnes by the end of the forecast, against the 1,471 tonnes under the Base Case. The weaker price trend results in a price elastic response from global jewellery consumption, which approaches the 2,400-tonne threshold by 2013, more than 200 tonnes higher than under the Base Case. While this will provide some price support (particularly on dips), the improvement will be insufficient to compensate for the decline in World Investment. Turning to supply, mine supply is still expected to grow in each year, although the gains are slight, particularly in 2013 as the retreat in prices takes its toll. The fall in prices will also bring about a sharp fall in scrap supply, although the level by the end of the forecast will still represent a historically high total and will still account for a little over 30% of total supply, compared to a norm in the mid-2000s (i.e. pre-crisis) of just under 25%. ###### **4.3 Developing World** 

The developing world has witnessed a material increase in scrap supply over the last decade, peaking at record levels in 2009, as gold prices rallied.  Scrap supply from this bloc of countries fell in 2010 despite the 26% rise in the average dollar gold price, with this unexpected change in trend due to a number of motivating factors. Firstly, consumers in several markets had become accustomed to the new, higher price level, particularly in an environment of lower price volatility and were therefore often reluctant to liquidate gold assets with expectations of yet higher prices to prevail.  Secondly, weakness in the US dollar meant that in many cases the gold price in domestic currency terms failed to register quite the same percentage gains as did dollar prices.  Finally, there was a degree of near-market depletion in several countries, with significant gold assets already liquidated, often during previous periods of buoyant prices. 

A key characteristic of most of these price sensitive markets remains the dominance of low labour cost and high carat jewellery.  Indeed, this low margin structure is the major reason why gold jewellery can often be viewed as quasi-investment vehicle in these markets, with consumers willing to “invest” in plain jewellery with the clear intention of selling the item back should the gold price move higher and a profit be obtained. 

While these market characteristics remain broadly in place, there has been a slow but nevertheless noteworthy shift within traditional styles away from heavy plain designs to light weight items and an increase in the use of stones to lower the precious metal content.  Rising gold prices remain the chief catalyst for this transformation as manufacturers in the last few years have attempted to maintain retail price points to attract a declining consumer base. Nonetheless, we would be surprised if this trend were to completely reverse should prices begin a secular slide.  In addition, we have seen growth for more fashion focused high margin jewellery that is more ‘western’ in style.  Both these trends are potentially significant for scrap as lighter, gemset or branded pieces are less likely to be scrapped.
